payload.body: A chord is a human-made musical construct: a set of two or more pitches (notes) sounded simultaneously, whose members bear harmonic relations to one another. Parameters: (1) size — the number of constituent pitches: dyad (two), triad (three), seventh chord (four), ninth chord (five) and beyond; (2) quality — the intervallic structure among the members: major (root–major third–perfect fifth), minor (root–minor third–perfect fifth), diminished (root–minor third–diminished fifth), augmented (root–major third–augmented fifth); (3) inversion — the arrangement of the members by which a different member occupies the bass position, changing the surface harmony while preserving the chord's identity; (4) voicing — the specific octave placement and spacing of the members, which affects the chord's texture without changing its harmonic function. Persistence mechanism: standardized in Western music theory through harmonic analysis, taught in harmony and ear-training curricula, reproduced in performance practice through chord symbols in lead sheets and jazz charts, and maintained through the notation of figured bass and the modern chord symbol system (e.g., 'Cmaj7', 'Am7b5'). It is distinguished from a single note (which fixes one pitch; the chord fixes a set), from a scale (which organizes pitches sequentially into a framework; the chord presents them simultaneously), and from a melody (which unfolds pitches in time; the chord suspends them together). [formal: chorda | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

payload.body: A tree data structure is a human-made hierarchical data structure: a finite set of nodes in which one distinguished root node has zero or more child nodes, every non-root node has exactly one parent, and no cycle occurs — equivalently, a connected acyclic structure (an arborescence) rooted at the root. Parameters: (1) branching factor — the maximum number of children any node may have, unbounded in the general tree and restricted to two (left and right) in the binary specialization; (2) ordering — whether a node's children carry a left-to-right order (ordered tree) or form an unordered set; (3) labeling — the value, key, or payload attached to nodes; (4) height — the length of the longest root-to-leaf path. Persistence mechanism: specified in algorithm textbooks and formal specifications (the CLRS lineage), implemented in software libraries as node-link or array (heap) representations, and maintained as the canonical form of hierarchical data — database indexes (B-trees in relational engines), file-system hierarchies, document object models, and parse trees in compilers. It is distinguished from a graph (which allows arbitrary edges and cycles; the tree is its connected-acyclic, rooted special case), from a linked list (a single chain — a degenerate tree of branching factor one), and from the English word 'tree' (the lexical item, filed on the board as a WORD-referent entry; this entry is the data structure that word names in one of its senses, and the two persist independently of one another). [formal: arbor structurae | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

payload.body: Priming is a human-made cognitive construct: a psychological effect in which exposure to a stimulus (the prime) systematically influences the response to a subsequent stimulus (the target), independent of conscious awareness or intentional effort. Parameters: (1) prime modality — visual, auditory, semantic, or emotional; (2) prime-target interval — the time between prime exposure and target presentation, typically ranging from milliseconds to hours; (3) prime-target relation — the semantic, perceptual, or associative link that must hold between prime and target for the effect to occur; (4) repetition threshold — the number of prime exposures required to produce a measurable effect, which varies by modality and individual susceptibility. Persistence mechanism: operationalized through controlled experimental paradigms (masked priming, repetition priming, associative priming) in cognitive psychology labs, replicated across laboratories through standardized protocols (e.g., the lexical-decision task, the Stroop paradigm, and the primed naming task), and maintained through the cumulative evidence base reported in peer-reviewed research. It is distinguished from learning (which requires repeated exposure and produces durable change; priming can occur in a single trial), from expectation (which involves conscious prediction; priming operates below awareness), and from mere exposure (which changes preference through familiarity rather than response facilitation). [formal: praeparatio | substrate: mind | horizon: a session | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

payload.body: The interference beat is a human-made measurement technique and conceptual map of wave interference. When two coherent waves of frequencies f1 and f2 (with a small difference) superpose, the resultant amplitude varies periodically at the beat frequency |f1 − f2|, producing a regular swelling and fading — beating — of intensity that a listener or detector perceives. The natural interference is the territory; the construct is the human-authored map that names it, quantifies it, and exploits it. Parameters: (1) two superposed waves whose frequencies differ slightly; (2) the beat frequency — the amplitude-modulation rate |f1 − f2|, which directly reveals the difference between the two sources; (3) the exploitation — driving the beat frequency to zero to tune one source to another, or measuring an unknown frequency against a known reference by counting beats. Persistence mechanism: the technique persists through its invariant mathematical relation (beat frequency = |f1 − f2|), its standard use in instrument tuning, heterodyning, and frequency comparison, and its standing as a worked example in physics pedagogy across acoustics, optics, and radio. Distinct from the musical beat, which is the rhythmic temporal unit that organizes meter and serves rhythm — a pulse of emphasis, not an interference measure; the two share only a homographic name.
